```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Willingness to pay is much stronger and better anchored. A has six live self-serve competitors charging $67-$799 per filing, each with a cited pricing page, plus a Reddit quote of $800-$2,500 accountant fees for an annual return. B's only price anchor is Edition.ink at $5/month, and free open-source clones of the same product already exist.",
    "Acquisition economics favor A. B's cited Nextdoor CPC of $2-5 is roughly one full month of revenue at $5/month before any conversion loss. A's Meta CPL of $27.66, likely higher in finance, is still small against a $150-$300 one-time ticket.",
    "A's demand evidence comes from current communities of the target payer (r/USExpatTaxes, r/AmericanExpatsUK) describing recurring pain and quoting prices. B's demand evidence is newspaper letters from 2008, 2017 and 2022 complaining about content bloat, not about wanting a paid personalized product.",
    "B carries a structural legal risk in its core mechanic. Its brief says scraping and AI-rewriting local news sits inside active publisher copyright litigation. Its secondary payer, local publishers, is explicitly unvalidated, and its publisher channel is marked [unsourced].",
    "A's main risks are scope and compliance, and both can be reduced. A one-country-pair wedge, or a US-side-plus-local-guidance product, could reach a first paying customer within 90 days. B's core problem is differentiating from free and $5/month alternatives, and that does not shrink by narrowing scope."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's demand evidence: three reader letters (2008 LA Observed, 2017 Concord Monitor, 2022 Napa Valley Register) complaining about irrelevant sections or declining paper quality. None shows anyone willing to pay for a customizable edition. The Concord Monitor letter in fact questions paying $130 at all, which undercuts the consumer-payer hypothesis. The brief's '~9% of Americans pay for local news' figure has no link, so it counts as missing.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderately confident. B is weak on payer and differentiation. A's 90-day path is not proven: the brief gives no timeline for EFIN authorization or software acceptance testing. Local-country filing liability and the legality of making country-specific calls without a local advisor are open questions. The US-only fallback is crowded and commoditized down to $67. A wins mainly because it shows an existing paying market at meaningful prices, not because its own differentiator is validated."
}
```
